newsitem.title: HONG KONG: WEEK AHEAD - Asian stocks seen weak, jittery.
newsitem.headline: WEEK AHEAD - Asian stocks seen weak, jittery.

text.p: Asian stocks face the week bracing for a U.S. rate hike, battered by the Thai currency battle and beleaguered by general investor disappointment in the region's economic fundamentals.
Traders said Hong Kong remained the only safe bet in the region, with smaller markets suffering from this week's aggressive attack on the Thai baht.
Currency weakness has harmed overall market sentiment in Southeast Asia, with Malaysia, the Philippines and Indonesia all considered vulnerable to further speculative pressure.
"I don't think institutions are going to rush in and buy these markets," one head trader said. But he said some technical buying could emerge in the worst-hit markets, such as Thailand.
Tuesday's meeting of the Federal Open Market Committee, the policy-making branch of the U.S. Federal Reserve, could further damage already fragile sentiment in Asia, another trader said.

U.S. stocks and bonds fell sharply on Friday as robust economic news fanned fears that the Federal Reserve will raise interest rates at the meeting. The Dow Jones industrial average fell 138.88 points, or 1.89 percent, to 7,194.67.
TOKYO - The Tokyo stock market is braced for the outcome of the Fed meeting and a series of domestic corporate results this coming week, brokers said.

But as New York markets are seen to have largely discounted a possible 0.25 point rise in interest rates, U.S. stocks may be boosted if the Fed leaves rates unchanged and that would in turn support the Tokyo market, they said.
On Friday, the benchmark Nikkei 225 average finished at 20,324.73, up 521.95 points, or 2.64 percent, on the week.
HONG KONG - The rapid ascent in share prices over recent weeks has left the market open to some volatility early in the coming week as investors await a Fed decision, brokers said.
"There is a wait-and-see attitude," said Geoff Galbraith, institutional sales trader at NAVA SC Securities.
Optimism on Wall Street helped drive the Hang Seng Index to all-time highs last week, with the blue chip index hitting an intra-day record high of 14,167.01 points last Thursday.
Over the week, the Hang Seng Index gained 131.57 points, or 0.94 percent, to close at 14,062.37.
BANGKOK - Brokers were waiting cautiously for details of government measures to boost the savaged Bangkok stock market, which plunged to an eight-year low last week.

A trader at General Finance and Securities said the market needed a big package of new support measures to restore confidence after a harrowing week aggravated by heavy speculative attacks on the baht.
The SET Index lost 44.24 points, or 7.3 percent, in the past week after dropping 54.67 points, or 8.3 percent, a week earlier. It ended on Friday at 561.19.
BOMBAY - Indian blue chips are seen range bound in the coming week as a looming rise in government-set oil prices overshadows fresh demand, traders said.
"The oil price hike is like a hanging sword over the market," said Ketan Jhaveri, chief dealer at Kotak Securities.
India's coalition government's steering committee meets on May 25 to raise prices of oil which it imports but sells to domestic customers at below world prices.
Bombay's top 30-share index ended the week down 9.70 points down to 3,759.64.
KUALA LUMPUR - Malaysian stocks are expected to start the week on a strong note before gains were capped on concerns about the Malaysian ringgit, dealers said.
"I see the upside for next week being capped. Next week should have a good beginning, but it will probably end down on the week," said Ralph Dixon of the international division of T.A. Securities.
For the week, the Composite Index of 100 large-capitalised stocks fell 65.46 points, or 5.91 percent, from the previous week. It ended on Friday at 1,041.91 points.
JAKARTA - Indonesian stocks are seen mixed in the coming week on growing concern over domestic political tensions ahead of the May 29 general election, analysts and brokers said.
On Friday, the Jakarta composite index closed at 657.07 points against the previous week's close of 673.99.
MANILA - Philippine shares are seen falling further on U.S. rate jitters and fears Thailand's financial woes could spill over into Manila, traders said.
"People would just want to get out ahead of the Fed meeting and there's still the Thai baht scare," said Noel Reyes, vice-president at Anscor-Hagedorn Securities.
The main index fell 54.96 points on Friday, closing at a year-low of 2,576.13. Week-on-week, the index shed nearly four percent from the previous week's 2,671.39 points.
SINGAPORE - The outlook for Singapore stocks was mixed with the market battling to recover the ground lost during the baht crisis while investors anxiously awaited news on U.S. rates.
"We might do a bit of a rebound, but it's really difficult to say when," a dealer at a local brokerage said.
The Straits Times Industrials Index ended at 2,060.50 on Friday, down 5.71 points on the previous week's close.
TAIPEI - Taiwan shares are expected to firm in the coming week as political worries gradually ease after Premier Lien Chan announced his resignation, effective in July.
"As political worries are easing, the index likely will be in a firming trend," said Michael Hung, an independent analyst.
On Saturday, the index closed down 59.33 points, or 0.73 percent, to 8,141.12, down 1.6 percent from a week earlier.
SEOUL - South Korean shares are seen moving higher in the coming week on the yen's appreciation against the U.S. dollar.
Foreign interest in Korean equities had increased with aggressive bidding reported for premium core blue chips in the over-the-counter market, one trader said.
The index closed at 706.25 on Saturday, up 27.27 points points, or four percent from the previous week's 678.98.
SYDNEY - Australian shares look set to continue strengthening with the key resources carrying the market.
The All Ordinaries index ended up 0.5 percent at 2,538.1 for both the day and the week after touching a record high 2,540.4 on Tuesday and a locking in a record close on Friday.
While the big banks came off the boil as pressure on margins was confirmed, investors bought up the miners as they considered the flow-on to commodities from growth in major economies.
WELLINGTON - The New Zealand top-40 share index ended the week virtually unchanged at 2,314.84 points and brokers expect the market to continue moving sideways in the coming week.
"The near-term outlook is pretty much the same. I can't see the market going too far from here," said Merrill Lynch broker Tim Koller.
